blocks.x: The 19th? The 19th, yeah. October the 19th, 1966. We're interviewing Chink Martin. Bill Howard. We're interviewing Chink Martin. Leonard Ferguson's apartment. This is Dick Allen property. This is Bill Russell.
What's your name? Leonard Ferguson. This is 707 St. Peter's Street. New Orleans.
You got all the information now, huh? Yeah. October 19th, 1966.
Interviewing Martin Abraham Sr. known professionally as Chink Martin.
Okay. Look at that, I'm the lad. Here we go, the thing in the old age.
So this is an ancient Roman movement one time ago, later on like this.
Yeah. What was your first instrument then? A guitar or a mandolin?

No, the guitar was my first instrument. The guitar was the very first. Yeah. I had one of the best professors, in fact. Well, that was years ago. You might remember, I don't forgot it was in what city it was, but the Queen's own band from Spain, New Mexico came down here. And he happened to be the baritone player, the brass baritone player. Baritone player. And he was a guitarist. When I say he was a guitarist, he was one of the finest, like that. Well, when the band went back, he stood here. What was his name? Francisco Quinones. Francisco Quinones. That was his name, Francisco Quinones. And I mean, that fellow was, he was out of this world. I seen him not because he was a drinker. He used to love to drink. And I'm telling you, sometimes he'd be just wobbling, staggering over the chair. But you'll never know it by his plan. And of course, he didn't play jazz, I'll admit that. He played nothing but waltzes and tangos naturally. So the standard style of rhythm. And operas and marches and things of that kind and operas. You know what I mean? But he was wonderful. How old were you when you heard him? Oh, gee. That was about when I was around 10, 11 years old. Well, we happened to be living in the same Bowden House at the time. It was a Filipino that was used to run it. It was a restaurant in a Bowden House, you see. Here in New Orleans? Yeah. Right on the ice line between Royal and Charters. Right across the street from Bracato's Ice Cream. Oh, yeah. And well, he started to learn some of the boys are playing and I happened that I was one of them. And he said, well, I got along all right. Until he'd seen that I was progressing pretty fast. And he says, well, now speaking about, now we're going to turn this around, speaking about Jack Lane. Jack Lane gave me the name of Chink Morton. And I always did say that he was the cause of Chink Morton giving me that name that it stuck to me, that he was the first one. But when I come to realize and think about it, it was not. It was this Mexican professor. Oh, he did. In Spanish, he used to call me in place, a call of Martin, which is more than in Spanish. He would call me Chinito. That means China. Oh, yeah. Yeah. The little Chinaman. Yeah. The little Chinaman. Yeah. The little Chinaman. Yeah. See. So he really was the first one that done it, you see. Yeah. Well, anyway, when he said that I progressed so much, you know, and so fast on the guitar, he says, well, now, he says, listen, you're just wasting your talent. On something like this. He says, tell you what I'm going to do. He says, you've got to start to learn. On the next lesson, you're going to start to learn music. And he says, and I want to put you on the guitar. Well, that scared me to death. That was the last time he ever saw me. Oh. I never got around. When he started about, he was going to learn me music and he was going to put me on piano. Because at that time, when you would say piano, it seems to me it was an instrument, which not only to me, to everybody else, it seemed, that it was a girl instrument. That anybody, a man would sit down and play a piano, they'd call him a sissy. Which is the truth. Yeah, I've heard that. That is the truth. You'd sit down and a man sit down and play a piano like that, they'd call him a sissy. Now, that sounds funny, you know, it sounds like, well, that kind of frightened me and I said, no, I'll never make it like that. So that was it.
Not around chargers and Ursulines anyhow.

Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's right. Because I'll tell you, at that time, at that time in, say, Ursuline Street, you take Decatur Street, you take Dumaine Street. Well, some part of Royal, from, I would say, from Royal and Dumaine, you could say, all the way to Espinade Street was nothing but Mexicans. Mexicans, Puerto Ricans, and Spanish. Yeah. You see? Yeah. That's the only way. And I'm telling you that they were a tough crowd. Like, well, that was it.
Was that around the time of the Spanish-American War?
Oh, no. That was in some ways around, I would say, about 1908, 1907, something like that.
But they had been there for a while then. They were there when you were younger, too.

Oh, well, yeah. They had been there for years. Because it was well populated. That's all. Well, it's just the same thing as you take the French market. We call it the French market. You ain't got a Frenchman around there that I know of. All these Italians, you know? Yeah. They took over.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, just after the period you're talking about. Well, it's the same thing with the Mexicans, little by little, you know, they're scattered around. You understand? Sure. Now, finally, it's very seldom that you see any around. But at the time I was speaking about it, where you just parade around them three streets, like Oisline, Domain, Chauders and that, and that's all you would see was Mexicans.
Yeah. I think by the time World War I came along, the Italians had started getting in there, quite a few of them. Mm-hmm. Yeah, they did.
Do you speak Spanish?

Well, I did speak Spanish, but I'm ashamed of it now, because I haven't spoke Spanish for years, and I forgot a whole lot. Of course, if I listen at a conversation or something, I'll understand it. But for me to open up a conversation, I'll get started, because there's things that I would like to say, and I forgot them. I can't. You see?
Your parents were Mexicans or Spanish? No, my parents were Mexicans and Spanish.

Well, talking right about this same period, Tim, I know you told me one time that you, I don't know how much you made, but you started on the tuba, I think, when you were about twelve, and a year later you actually made a little money playing on the darn thing.

On the tuba? No, no. Yeah. Bass fiddle? No, that was on the guitar. On the guitar? On the guitar. Well, I'll tell you about that. You see, there was a, you know, always a system here with the high color, with the Mexicans and the Puerto Ricans. That's what you haven't got to there. Well, that vanished a long time ago. It's serenading. Mm-hmm. Say sometime about, say, 10 o'clock, maybe until 10, 12, 1 o'clock in the morning. Well, if they were going to serenade a mother or they were going to serenade a sweetheart or a wife or a friend or a friend or anything. a friend, even a friend. Naturally, they'd want to serenade them, to surprise them, and go over there and go to their door and sing. Well, some of the Mexicans that really knew how to play, well, they didn't need any compliments, they had it. But there's plenty of them that didn't do that, that's why I came in. They would come to me and say, we'd like you to be going to serenade such and such a place and we'd like you to play for us. Well, I'd just ask them what songs they were going to sing, actually, which is all Spanish, what songs they were going to sing and things like that. And they'd tell me. So I'd go with them. The senorita ever throw a roll? I'd give them the introduction and they'd start the same. They'd open up the doors and the windows and in no time they had a table spread out there with wine, food and everything you could mention. Like that. Just a serenade, you know? But mostly that I have played most than anything else. Now I don't know for what reason. But you might have heard it, they call it in English not a dove, but in Spanish they call it La Guadalurina. Which is mostly a love song.
I always get that one confused with La Paloma. Well, La Paloma too.

Oh, that's the dove. I still haven't listed as the dove. And they used to have another one, but that was very seldom played up because I believe it was a Puerto Rican. It's named Cuba. Oh, Cuban. Do you know what's called Cuba?

Yeah, yeah. I never heard that. I never heard that one. I don't know how it goes or anything. I don't know. Kind of piano style or what? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He used to make a parody of it. Well, they made a parody of it, like singing to, what would I say? It's not a wife, would you say it would be a mistress? They'd sing that. Let's see, wow, it went. I'll never think of that one, will we? Adios, adios, adios, pueblo querida. Estigo fiel, pues dándole a mi amor. Si acaso muero, mi amor ofano, aquí dejo la dueña de mi amor. En ad mis lechos lo pondré sonido, adonde pueda en la estación pasar. Si acaso muero, mi amor ofano, aquí dejo la dueña de mi amor.
That's nice. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I hear the parody, sure. It's a parody, isn't it? Yeah.
It's mostly, like I said, it's like singing to a mistress more than anything else, not to a wife, you see.
Now, your home was in the quarter when you were a young fellow doing this? Yeah, my home.

In fact, the time that I lived to be up until, I would say it, until I was up to 30 years old, I didn't move from Esplanade to Domaine. That was my quarters right there, from Esplanade to Domaine. No further up or no further down. Were you born right in that section? And from the riverfront to Rampart Street. Uh-huh.
Well, you find an area you like, why leave, huh? That's right.
Were you born right in that section, right here? No.
I was born in Bias St. John.
Oh, yeah.

I mean, when Bias St. John was Bias St. John, that's all they had but luggers there. The fishermen used to come from the lake, you'd come right through the bayou like that and land right there. The schooners. The schooners and the luggers and things like that, you know? Yeah. Yeah, that's quite, that's something quite a few years ago, too.
Used to come in right behind where the Municipal Auditorium is now, huh? Beauregard Square, what they used to call Congo Square. That's right.
Yeah. That's right. In the Caronelette Canal. Yeah. You know your birthday? Yeah. Oh, you mind my afternoon?
No, not at all. I was born the 10th of June, 1889. 1889. Wednesday, the 10th.
Now, how do you know that? I've heard this discussed. Now, how did you decide that's a... Well, first, that's the way that my Christmas paper was stated.

That's the date that's on your Christmas date? Yeah. But what I was to come to understand by my parents, that there was a mistake on there, because, you see, as a rule, they didn't christen the children at that time as fast as they christened them. Now, well, you can say if they were, if they would come to the royal and they were born, said today, maybe two or three weeks or maybe a month after they christened them. At that time, your children sometimes would be two or three years old before they christened them.
Yeah.

You see? And I happened to be three years old before they christened me. But they're still putting that paper, they're putting that paper, 1889, the day I was christened. Yeah, so... So, in fact, in place of being 77, I should be 80. Yeah, well, that's what I think. I think you're 80. That's what it is, but of course I can't claim that because it's got to be like in what? Mm-hmm. I had that argument with the union, too.
Yeah?

Yeah. I said, at that time, when they gave me my life card, I told them, I don't forgot what it was, I told them I was 62 or 63 at that time, see? Something like that, anyway, I can't think of it, so I'll fall back. And they went towards the papers and got it into the city hall and they found out that I was below that, of that age. And cut to find out, then I done had my card, life card, and I had to pay $27 more. That's a piece. So I could be straightened out with the union.
Oh. You were in the union for years, huh?
Yeah. That's the year I made my appearance, Jay. 1923. I made my debut, yeah.
Yeah, 1923, and it was 1923, 1922 or 1923 when I joined the local in number 10, in how you call it, in Chicago.

I see, you didn't join the union here, but after you went to Chicago, you mean? Yeah, I joined the one in Chicago. Well, that time, that would have put you up with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings then, at that time, in Chicago.
Did you have a hard time getting in the union then?

Well, it wasn't easy. See, these fellas, when they came, Rapolo, when he came down here, of course I'm not a well-educated man, I'm not an educated man, and then I was a young man, you know how a young person feels about it like that. Like they say, sometimes he don't even think about danger, he thinks about it after it's too late, you know. But he came down over to the house and he asked me if he'd like me to go to Chicago, join the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. So I told him, I says, well, Rapolo says, you know I'm not in the union. Oh, he says, we got that fixed, Jake. I says, you have? I says, what are you talking about? He says, oh, listen, he says, you don't have to, he says, I understand, you think you've got to go through examination. I says, that's right. You've got to go through an examination in Chicago to pass a union. Oh, he says, well, you've got all that fixed. But I'll be like, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Finish this? Oh, I think so. We're not in a great hurry. Jake, before we get too far.
Well, you were talking about the union. Yeah. How do you have to finish up that story?
What, about the union?
Yeah, the examination.

Well, I went off, well, after he came and saw me, he had me convinced that they had everything fixed in the union, that all I had to do was pay my fees and started to work. So, when I went up there, I found out different. They never had anything fixed. I was on my own. So, I went there and reported to the union. They said, well, all right. We'll send you a card for examination. I said, ain't this nice. This is really pretty. But, I figured, like they told me, that they had everything fixed. You see? So, I didn't worry about it. I said, well, if they got everything fixed, I ain't got nothing to worry about. You see? Anything I'll do, it's all right. I went there and reported to the union. I said, well, all right. We'll send you a card for examination. You see? You see? Ain't this nice. This is really pretty. You see? But, I figured, you know, that like they told me, that they had everything fixed. You see? So, I didn't worry about it. I said, well, if they got everything fixed, I ain't got nothing to worry about. You see? Anything I'll do, it's all right. So, I went there and there was about, oh, I would say, because that's a big local, they must have had about 200 people and they're musicians. To be an audience for your...
No.

They just happened to be there, huh? No, to be there for the past examination themselves, you see? I am by myself. You see? New members. I just got in. New members. So, they had a little stand there with four members on there that writes the cards for you. In fact, they were the, what would you call them, the professors or something. If you pass or you don't. Right, they were the judges. The judges. Yeah. And they had a piano there and a professor right there with you. See? They called my name and I took my bass and I went up and the professor started turning the pages on them. A string bass. Now, remember this. At that time, I was playing a three string bass, not a four string bass. Three string bass. So, follow me. I was playing a bass. So, when I went up, the professor at the back, you know, and the instructor said, you know, is that what you play? Three strings on the bass? I said, yes sir. He looked at me, you know. He said, all right. So, he turned to music and says, okay, one, two, three, four. See? So, I'll play it anything. He tapped me. I'll make it short. He tapped me on my shoulder. And he says, listen. He says, I'll tell you what you do. You go back home. He says, you didn't just play that right. I guess they didn't want to tell me that I didn't know how to read and what they were telling the truth. I didn't know a note as big as this bell. So, he said, you go home and he says, when I think you're right, he says, I'll send you another card for examination. So, that was the finale. So, I knew right well that I made a fool out of myself, you see? So, I packed up my bass and going down and I forgot what was the name of the secretary there. Bankard. Bankard. Bankard was the secretary. And he seemed like he took a life into me, you see? When I came down to fly the steps on the half of the flight, see because I was up on the second floor, he says to me, he says, how'd you make it out? And Gus says, not so good. He says, why? I says, well, I'm going to tell you the truth. I says, Mr. Bankard. I can't read or know what I don't know. I know it as big as this building. I said, them fellas fooled me and they told me that everything was, they had everything to fix here. That anything I do, I says, I don't read no music. Oh, he says, no. He says, you can't play a cymbal or anything. I says, well, even at that I would have to know time. I have to know music. He says, well, yeah, that's true too, he says. Well, he says, Abraham, is there anything that I can do to help? He says, let me know and he says, I'll do it, see? So, I thought a while and I says, well, I'll tell you what you do. I says, will you give me another chance and send me your card so I can come back here? He says, but you can't wait. He says, Abraham, what that good that's going to be? He says, that's not going to do you no good if you didn't pass now. He says, in a couple of days you can't pass over again. I says, I think I can do it. Because I took notice, they had about, oh, they must have had about five or six of them before me. And it was only three numbers in that book that the professor was changing, you see? Which I didn't pay, it means they told me everything was fixed, I didn't pay no attention to it, see? I says, I think I can do it. He looked at me and he says, well, he says, I wish I had John Noyiff. He says, you really got courage. He says, but I'll tell you what I'll do. He says, I'll send you a card. So, I says, I'll tell you what you do. Will you do me a favor? He says, what is it? I says, try to put me last as far back as possible. He says, why, Chinky? I says, because I took notice. He says, I told him, I was frank with him. I said, I took notice, there's only three numbers that the professor changes on there in that book. And it's nothing but six, eight temples. I says, there's march temples. Well, I knew that from playing guitar from the professor, you know. He would learn me how to play guitar. I knew the difference between waltzes and fox strats and everything else, you see? Forch temples comes up. He says, well, what is the reason that I think I said? Because I'm going to pay attention with that. And the deductions that they're taking, and I'll be able, I think I'll be able to do it. He looked at me, he says, Chinky. He says, Abraham, because you didn't call me Chinky. There ain't no one would change. He says, Abraham, I'll send you a card. He says, if you've got the nerve enough to come up here, he says, and go over that again. He says, I've got to know the courage to send you another card. I said, well, all right. So, it was about four or five days, and he sent me a card. He did something. So I went up there. And sure enough, he left me way back, you see. But in the meanwhile, there was a few strings that was pulled. Because when they seen that I was jammed and everything else, they introduced me to the hires, you know, to the big shots and things like that, you know. I don't want to mention names. I know their names. But it's no use going through that. So anyway, I went up there in five days. So I kept my ears open with that introduction. Because that's how you play, was the intro. They don't let you play a whole number. Just the introduction to see if you know how to read. Yeah. And I kept that thing right straight in my ears. It was burning my ears, you see. So I took notice of one number that they played. It went, and I'll never forget it.
That was the bass.

Yeah. I said, man, I wish I was lucky that he would put that up. Because I had that more insecure than the other two, you see. So I went up there in the car. Boy, it was my rock. He put out that God-dannable. You see what I was doing? And he went, he went, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. He says, hold on. He says, hey Brian. He says, wasn't you here four or five years ago? I said, yeah, yes sir. He says, well, man, he says, why didn't you do that before? I says, well, I don't know. You're a little excited and nervous. I said, a big audience like this and you say. He says, my boy, he says, you don't understand. He says, in the profession you're in, that's what you're going to need people. You're going to need audience. You've got to have courage. You've got to have spunk to go up there and meet them. He says, if you're going to get nervous, he says, you ain't going to do any good. He says, give the man a call.
Very good. Very good. Very good. Very good.

Well, before we get too far up towards Chicago and later dates, I just wanted to ask you one question, Chaint, that I've wondered about because I've heard people make some statements. As I do a little arithmetic here now, I would say that this time that you're doing your serenading under the window and all this kind of stuff over on Ursuline Street, if it wasn't right around the turn of the century, it certainly wasn't very long after it, was it? Pretty close afterwards there, after 1900 came in. Oh, yeah. So, in other words, you were familiar with the music scene, naturally being a young man interested in music, you paid attention to what was going on around town. Oh, yeah. There are a lot of people, I think mostly from places other than New Orleans and mostly non-musicians, who are of the opinion that for many, many years only the colored people played anything that we would today describe as jazz, and that at a very late date, a few white people began to imitate the colored people. When you were a young fellow coming along around the turn of the century, was it strictly colored people then, or also white people?

No, that was really wrong. I never did want to come out with that discussion, because you have so many people that contradict you about that. But when they tell you that a colored man can play a better strict temper than a white man, don't let nobody kid you about that. That really is a bad face lie. It's just somebody that brought that up, you understand what I mean? And it's just a reputation, more of a reputation than anything else. Because I played with bands, I played with bands in 1900, late, up until this present day. And I mean every one of them was strict temper. Now, I played with colored men that I had trouble with. Now, believe me when I'm telling you that, I'm not exaggerating, I'm not taking anything away from you. You understand what I mean? Sure. Because I'm not... ... ... ...
I don't know, we're speaking about the temper of the colored and the white man.
Do you find that the colored people tend to rush or drag or what?

Well, no. You see what happens here, I'll tell you. It seems like everything else. And this racial affairs that we have right now, that the colored people are trying to imitate the white. Just the opposite of what the other people face. In place of keeping to their own style, they're trying to imitate the white. And imitation is bad and it's no good. Because you never can be the original. I don't care how good you are, you'll never beat the original.

Al, just let me digress one moment. Al Rose told me something the other night. You know how much these Japanese boys over here, how much they imitate the George Lewis band. And that clarinet player thinks George, of course, is the most wonderful thing in the world. And just to show you how far imitation can go sometimes, he had a bottle of Dr. Tishner's antiseptic, you know, in his clarinet case. And somebody asked him, why in the world are you carrying a bottle of Dr. Tishner's in your clarinet case? What's it for? He says, he doesn't know what it's for yet. He's trying to find out. But when George Lewis came to Japan, he had a bottle of Dr. Tishner's in his clarinet case. Dr. Tishner's antiseptic.

No, we're going right back to where we started from. Now we're speaking about rhythm, tempo, kick, swing. You understand? Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. Now, the people, intelligent people are broad-minded. It's only but the ignorant people that never sits down to try to figure this out. But if the intelligent people, if they just sit down and figure this out for themselves, they're going to find out that I'm telling you the truth. Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. Now, you can learn a poison music, right? Can you learn a tempo?
Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. Well, if you get them to think about it, they can improve, I think.

Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. Well, they could improve. But could you knock it in their head to keep tempo? Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. No. That would be less. That's something that you can't learn a poison. It's got to come from under your heart. Dr. Tishner's antiseptic. In other words, you've got to have that feeling. If you haven't got that feeling, nothing happens. Now, I'll show you what I mean about that. We're coming right back to this old professor, Francisco Quinones. When he was learning us, he had about, let's see, it was Mossoy and King, myself. There was three of us. And I don't forgot the other fellow. There was four of us, I know. But I can't think of the other. Whoever the other poison is. Now, you know what they call a metronome? That is just like your clock. You can't beat it. You understand? Now, what he used to do with us, he used to take this and say, all right, here's the metronome. In Spanish. Uno, dos, tres, cuatro. Uno, dos, tres, cuatro. Uno, dos, tres, cuatro. Uno, dos, tres, cuatro. Now, he said, take it from there. Plum, plum, plum, plum, plum, plum. On the guitar. Turn your face. Away from it. See? And he smothered the microphone. So you couldn't hear it. Couldn't hear it. But keep on playing. Plum, plum, plum, plum, plum, plum, plum. Then he'd take it off. And we're all in. If it was out, if it was too fast or too slow, he says, see? He says, that don't lie. He says, that's what I want you to do. Well, it seems like I don't want to, you know what I mean. I don't want no flowers or nothing like that. But he used to praise me and sometimes he used to call a bunch of friends and show them what I could do. He used to take that mic, three, four tempo, waltz tempo, two, four tempo, any kind of tempos at all and set that mic. See? Like that. I'd go as far as getting the tempo from there, keep on playing and go to the next room and come back and be playing with that thing when he uncovers it. Now that's how strictly I played tablet. That's why he changed his mind. When he seen that I progressed so good, that's why I said before, he wanted me to play piano. But when he played, he wanted me to play piano and he wanted me to start reading music, I quit. That was it.

That was the final. Well, from those early days then, they had, did they have white musicians playing what today we could have called early jazz? They had white musicians. The boys? At the turn of the century now we're talking about, they had white musicians playing jazz then. Now what were they called?
1900. Now, 19, well.
Or say 1905 along in there.

Well, now I can tell you about, let's see, 1905. No, I would say from about 1908 or something like that. Because what do I remember, I couldn't be no more than about nine or ten years old at the time. When I heard the first, when I heard the first jazz band, white jazz band, and that was the High Rollers. High Rollers? High Rollers.
Well, that would have been about 1900, I think, when you were nine or ten years old.
Well, it could be. It's so far back. I remember, I'm thinking way back. I'm trying to think way back.
Was it a marching band or?

No. Was it a regular, it was supposed to be, but at that time we didn't call it a jazz band. We called it Ragtime band. Ragtime band. You understand? There was no jazz band. Yeah. That only came out lately, it was jazz. Because, to tell you the truth, at that time, if you said a word of jazz in front of women folks, they'd knock your head off. Bad word. Because they took it as a bad meaning, a bad word. Of course, I can't explain myself like I should. You know? Yeah. You understand what I'm talking about? You understand what I'm talking about? I understand that. Well, that's the idea. They used to call it Ragtime band, you see? But that really was the first white band that I can remember of here. Had you had a hundred bands earlier? Yeah, I mean that was a full band, a full band because they had about, oh I would say about eight men, seven, eight men.
What instruments? What did they play?

They played guitar. One of them was Johnny Fernandez. The other one was Johnny Guitar. He played guitar. Bullwinkle. Wait, Bullwinkle. What did Bullwinkle play? I believe it was drums. That's a mistake. Let's not leave him out forever. Bullwinkle played drums. And Pete, wait a minute now. The Kornak player you're talking about? Pete Dentron. Yeah, I heard of him. You heard of him. Pete Dentron played trumpet. Gallaty used to play trombone, but Val trombone. And Parashe. Oh yeah, I know who you're talking about. We used to call him a different name.
He's a cousin of Pujol you're talking about. Pujol, that's right. Pujol. Pujol. Pujol.
You see, I'm starting to show too far back. I'm starting to show.
Well, your earliest recollections though, they were already white people playing jazz.

I know he went to a different name but Pujol. But his name was Palaszczuk. You see what I mean? Yeah. But we gave him the name of Pujol. I don't know how to call him, but that was it. Now, that was the men that really played in the high roles. Now, you had the...
Which one was the leader, Tink? Did you remember him? Bill Gallaty. Bill Gallaty.

Old man, not because he's got a son. We've got a Bill Gallaty plays now. Plays a trombone. Yeah, that's his son. Well, that's his son. He's worked with our band from time to time. Well, that's his son. Well, he's daddy. Because they used to own a dairy. He used to be a dairyman. He used to own a dairy. See? Well, that's all that I could think of. And then, following that was Jack Lane's band. And from Jack Lane's band was Frankie Christian, which I happened to play with them too. I played with Autumn. I kept on going, thank God. With Frankie Christian. And...

Well, the reason I ask, Tink, is that every once in a while somebody comes, usually somebody from up north somewhere that is an expert of one kind or another. And I've even had some of them actually tell me that until even around 1920, in the early 20s, that nobody ever heard of any white people playing jazz. And, of course, not having been around myself, I have no personal experience, but it didn't sound right to me. That's why I wanted to ask you.

No, listen. Believe me when I tell you this. There is no man or no woman that can learn a poison how to play temple. Force temple is concerned. It's got to come from under the heart. In other words, I'll tell you what. I'll tell you what. Now, I'm going to put a, for instance, right now. If you know how to dance, you're going to keep temple. If you see, if that man is playing faster or slower, can't you tell if he's breaking that temple? If he's slow enough or if he's going ahead? Yeah.
Am I right or wrong?

Am I right or wrong? Yeah. Well, them is the only people that knows temple. The ones that's got to dance. And if I do say it, I used to love to dance. Yeah. Of course, I don't do it now. It's years that I haven't done it.
Well, what you don't like now is the boy and the girl stand clear across the room from each other.

But don't let nobody kid you. They don't let nobody kid you or nobody else. That's something that you can't teach nobody. It's got to come. It's got to be born in you. That's all the story. But for all, it's like plenty of them, you know, the critics are talking about the colored man playing more rhythm and playing strictly tempo than the white. No, don't let nobody kid you. That's been my life. You had the biggest bands I did before. Well, Isen Jones and way back. Like that. Okay. Now that big, there was no jazz. It was beautiful arrangements. But just listen at that temple. Yeah. You couldn't break that away from the men. You mean to come and tell me that that men were in there from the colored people? No, that don't make any sense. No, it really don't make no sense. Because I've been playing tempo, I can remember myself that when, as far as back, that I can remember. I was nothing but a kid. And you know what I used to do? I don't know if you ever saw a song that was kind of a wire that used to go around your neck with a harmonica. Like that. I used to play the harmonica and take my mother's watch stuff. And boy, I was going to town. And I was that small that I couldn't carry the watch stuff. Yeah. That's what I'm saying. There's no such thing if the colored people learn as a temple. Because it's like I'm saying, there's nobody can learn you that. And now, you can believe me when I'm telling you, that the colored people, as far as it's concerned, they're losing more tempo than the white people are doing. Now, pay strictly attention to that now, and I'm going to show you that I'm right about that. I think they rush. I think the drum is rush. Now, right. You're right. Now you come and do it. Sounds to me like they do, but I never say anything. You know why? I'll tell you why. You know why? I'll tell you why. You know why? Dick, I'll tell you why. The changing of the music. In other words. You see, the old time drum players hardly used the sticks on the snare drum with fan brushes. In other words, they were playing with going. No drum solo or nothing. Now, they're taking the drums and going ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum ba dum. See how many kicks they can make on a bass drum. In other words, they're playing a solo drum. They're not playing drums. And there's no man, I don't care who he is, and how fast he is, that he's going to start kicking a drum like that and trying to make too many beats in the measure of the music like that, that he's keeping tempo. He can't do it. I don't care who he is.

I always felt sorry for the bass player in some of these modern jazz bands because he's the only one that's keeping the tempo. The drummer is playing strictly counterpoint, making bombs bursting in air.

That's right. The bass man is the only one making dum ba dum ba dum. And I will say it brought forth the best of the bass. The drum player is making a ribbit. The bum bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing bing. That's not helping the rhythm at all. Yeah. Oh well. Well, I guess that's it. How were the tempos in the old times? Did they play everything so fast? No, the old tempos was mediocre. That's what I learned. That's mediocre. That's what I want to get into. The same thing. Now the man I spoke to was Sante Piccolo, our trombone player. Well, we came in an argument like that, that to play jazz and to make the people excited or something like that, you've got to play fast. Now, here, now we're going to face something like this. Now we know that everybody, mostly of them anyway, they love Louis because man Louis Armstrong, they think he's the greatest. Okay. We leave it go at that. So now, you take the white bands, even up to Disneyland. Of course, I will say this year, looked like they kind of cooled down a little. But the previous year, everything was... Now that's what they call Dixieland Band. Alright. Well we all play it like that. Understand well. Well as a rule, they put Louis Armstrong as king of jazz. He's the last float to come out the bay. And you know what he's playing? Hello, Dolly. Hello, Dolly. He makes the white bands look cheap. According to the applause that the people has given Louis Armstrong. And I know doing well that the bands that they got out there, it's better than Louis Armstrong has got. But it's just that swing and that tempo, that feeling. In other words, when you play music, you've got to play music where people feel it. It's not that just blah blah blah blah. You've got to play music that the people feel. Now we played over at the famous store. Now Sandra Pecor is playing there and all he's playing there, which I call it, you know, with all respects they're playing there. They're all good musicians and everything. But the tempo they're playing is more ballet house, what they call ballet hall music than anything else. Now we used to play, when we used to play with Shokin, we used to play the right tempo. There's where you can tell the difference of the people, feels it or like it. When we used to play, you see the people take their hands and hit it on the counter. Keep them tempo with the music. If not, it will be a problem. That's what you got to feel. That's what you got to feel. That's what you got to feel. That's what you got to look at. When them people are doing that, they're feeling it. Naturally, if you're playing fast or something, they give you a hand, they know you're trying to do your best and they give you a hand, it's wild. But it's not that they like it, because you're not making them feel it. You understand?

That's what I was telling you one other time, Tink, you may remember, why I kind of differentiate between what some people think of as Dixieland today and what we think of New Orleans jazz, all this fast stuff that they call Dixieland today, that's what I say, that's the Ringling Brothers, Barnum and Bailey version of New Orleans jazz.

That's not the real New Orleans jazz. No, we played, what was that affair that we played when we got, when all the actors and that came out, was it a hard fun or whatever it was? When we played with the band?
Oh, Save Your Symphony. Huh? That was the drive to save the symphony.
Ah, oh.
Victor Borghi was the star of the show.
Now, now there's boys that's really knowing, they're popular and everything else, and they've got plenty of work and everything else. But that tempo is fast tempo.
Oh, yeah.

How about the last cross? Now, let me show you. Now, they're all musicians. All right. We get there and we start to play. Naturally, they played one number and we play another number. Well, the boys in the band could see what they were doing. This is what they were doing on the other side of the stage.
Yeah.
Keeping the hardwood upper. That goes to show you we made even them feel it.
Oh, they've always been some of our greatest fans. The Lansdrasse have always been the fans.

You see? And they're one of our greatest fans. They'll tell you that. Yeah. As far as a dance band, they'll tell you that. Yeah. That's why I'm saying, when you play music you've got to play it with feelings. It's a different profession from anything else. If you play music and it's blah, nothing comes out. You've got to play it from under your heart. Like the old man used to tell me that Francisco Quignones one day he was playing a solo on a guitar and I told him, I says, pro, I says, my God, I says, I really would be proud if I play just as half as good as what you do. He turns around to me and he tells me, he says, listen, Chinito, that was in Spanish because he couldn't speak English. He says, remember these words, what I'm going to tell you. He says, I'm an old man. He says, and you're nothing but a child. He says, but remember this because as long as you live, you're going to remember it. And believe me, he did. He says, it's not what you do, it's how you do it. He says, and never forget this. He says that everything you do, make it come from under here. He says, and you'll never go wrong. And believe me, up until this day, I'll remember that. And he was right. Yeah.
Wondering about the old time bands, were they much different than today? How were they made up? What instruments did they use when you were, I say, 1908 or 1910? When you started?

Well, you see, that's what made me drop the guitar because I couldn't make a living on it. The only thing I could do is just, like I say, to play for the Mexicans for their singings, for their serenades, I'd make a few dollars. But it was not in demand. See, because at that time there was no such thing as amplifiers like you have right now. For real. Well, if you put a guitar in a band with brass like that, you wouldn't hear it from here to that wall. You understand what I mean? Now, that's why the banjos came in, which gave more volume. You understand? Well, you know, the band was a big one. But, even with that, mostly of the bands never used that. The only thing that the bands would use is the trumpet, the clarinet, the trombone, the bass and the drums. No piano? No, no accompaniments at all. In which it was hard. Because, in other words, for the bass man it was hard because he didn't hear no after beat at all. You see what I mean? Yeah. And the band was the drum.
Well what kind of a part did you play in those days? Did you run up and down the chords? Well, no, no.

That's where, you see, that's where I want to try to tell you about this. Plenty of people say that I play a strange bass than the rest of the men. Because mostly the bass players right there, they play strictly bass. You understand? Yeah. And naturally it's just either one to the measure or two to the measure. You understand? Never make four. You're making a mistake when you made that at that time. Right. Because there was no such thing as a kick. You understand? So, I started to figure myself. I said, well this sounds empty. There's something really which I didn't know myself. To tell you the truth, I didn't know myself. But I knew there was something missing that the band sound empty. So in place of playing just the bass as it should be played, I made the full chords on the bass. In place of making, say for instance you're making bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum. Make the full chords to keep the band full. You understand what I mean?
But everybody didn't do that back then.

No, no, it's just strictly two to the measure, which is an old time rag time band. But, you see this is the idea. You're making that one, two, one, two, one, two, one, two, one, two. Well you find out that it's empty, they're submissing on it. So they started with that in place of one, two, one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, one, two. Give you that lift. You understand that? That's all there's to it.
When did you start doing that? Huh? When did you start doing that?
Well I started doing that for almost two or three years after I started playing bass.
Before you went to Chicago and all that. Huh? Before you went to Chicago. Yeah.

No. I started to realize, I said, well dear, there's something empty here. You know, you would just hear the lead and the trombone once in a while coming in. Then, at that rate, another thing that I got to say, we never had the trombone players that you got today. See? Which made it a little empty. Because at that time I'm speaking about the trombone players, which, what they claim now is tailgate, they're not playing tailgate. The tailgate trombone players, that's all they used to make. The tailgate trombone players, that's all they used to make. More slimes than anything else. That's what you would call tailgate. Now they're giving you that. They're making more notes in a measure than the trumpet is making.
What kind of a part did the clarinet play?
The clarinet player always did play the variations. I'll admit I did. But they do learn? They tried to fill in as much as they possibly could.

Can I digress for a moment, Bill, on this very point, getting kind of modern now. When Pete Fountain was Al Hurt's clarinet player and then he went out and got on Lawrence Welk and so on. He really never did come back to the band. And Pee Wee Spadalera went into Al Hurt's band. And I was walking down Bourbon Street to buy my paper, as I do many a night, and I ran into Pee Wee standing on the corner outside the club down there. And he had been with Al about two weeks at that time. I said, Pee Wee, how do you like playing with Al Hurt? And he said, well I really don't know what to play. And of course he was a very capable clarinet player and I wasn't expecting any answer like that. And I said, well what do you mean you don't know what to play? And he said, Al plays all of his notes and then he plays all of mine. Yep.
There are variations too.

You see, the idea of making a band and having a band like that, is for a band to play together. That's what makes a band. It don't have to be ex-boys and stars. As long as they play together. It's just like you take a football team or a baseball team. They got to work together and they got to play together. If one of them is going to show more than they can show the rest of them what he can do and what he can do, then you break up the team. Well that's the same thing with music. If the trumpet player is going to play a lead, play a lead. You know the clarinet player plays the variations, play the variations. The trombone plays the trombone parts, he knows. That's the counter melody of the music. You understand what I mean? Don't try to play with the trumpet is playing or try to play with the clarinet is playing. You understand that? That's the thing that makes a band. But that's what plenty of these bands can understand.

That's one reason, Chink, the band you're playing in now is called the Night Owls, because we want ensemble. We think that if you start out with so-and-so and his orchestra, right away you've lost the ensemble because it's a showcase for one man.
Fifty years ago did they have a lot of solos? They start out an ensemble and everybody plays the same.

For, listen, for is drum solos. I'm going to put it on a drum. That only came a few years back as drum solos. Then a drum player never did play a drum solo in my years. All he done was play drums and give that band the tempo. When that band hit one, two, that leader hit one, two, three, four, there he was. If it wasn't with the sticks, it was the brushes, but mostly the brushes. You understand? Because to tell you the truth, when you make a band and you want to hear the full harmony of the band and hear every instrument, the drums are supposed to be felt, not hoired. Because that's an instrument that can outdrown any other instrument. And when you start forcing those blowing instruments, then you ain't got nothing. Because then you're expanding the men and they can't play what they want to play. You see, myself, we played at the ringside with Sharky. And we had one, I'll tell you how good that band was. We had Charlie Cadela, Charlie Cadela, Harry Shields, Sharky, Joe Caparro. What's the boy, that drummer that Drowning himself? What do they call him again? Drowning himself? Yeah. Drummer? I don't remember any drummer.
Who did he play with?
He played with us.
Who's this band, the Sharky, the Chester? Yeah, but I mean did he play with Bersdorf too? No. That must have been before I came to town, Chief.

Oh yeah, yeah. What was his name? I can't think of it. Well anyway, from him we turned to Shaline. Then I doubled up on tuba and string bass. Freddie Newman was playing piano. Joe Caparro was playing guitar. Now, they gave me the business of being the man to run the band. They were the leader because I told them I didn't want anything about leadership. And up until today I don't. But I told them just what I would like for them to do and play. And I told the drummer, I says, fan brushes at all times. I says, and don't get wild, we want to feel it. And that's all. You see? Well we played at the ringside and we stood there for about four or five years at the ringside playing for Pete Hoyman. And.
Bands today? No, no, they didn't sound like the bands today because mostly of them, to tell you the truth, they were not accomplished musicians.

There's many things that I went through that naturally you couldn't put on tape because you never played in front of women. But I'm telling you, I played with some rough elements there, I'm telling you. Especially with that Jack Reed song, that Patrick. Oh, you ain't got that on, eh?
Oh, yeah, well you don't have to, you said you weren't going to tell it before it went on anyway. You want to take it off and you tell us something and turn it off.

I was waking with Johnny Byerstoff at the Tokyo Garden. And he, you see, his father used to be a swine in the Sharmogrot. The Sharmogrot of the Sharmogrot. Well, he was one himself. Byerstoffer. Yeah, Byerstoffer, the trumpet player. That was before he went off and he left the city, see. So, naturally his dad had got our band to go and travel all around the country with the Shriners. They had made a tour all around the country with the Shriners, see. So, every time that we would go in a different city, we'd have to get off the train and the band and pray to get the Shriners together, see. To receive the new delegates that was coming on, see. So, I don't forget what city it was. We stopped there and we got off. And I had that great big tour that I used to have, you know. That's Harry BJ. That bell was that big one. I had it especially made. The tour was a Suzaphone. Suzaphone.
It was a Suzaphone, see. Is that a double B-flat?

No, E-flat. But it was a double E. It was a double E, see. Big one. Yeah. So, we got off in this special city. I don't remember where it was. And like I said, we got the plan to get the new delegates in there, you know. So, the band is playing. And I see old man Biles Stoffer. He's looking at me like that, you know. He's doing this, you see. He don't say nothing, you see. Got through playing. He said, Jim, do you feelin' alright? I said, yeah, why? He says, I don't know. He says, but I don't hear that tuba. And boy, if I do say that I was young, at that time I had win. Yeah. Because I played it with, what, 16, 20 men. You could hear that tuba above the band. Anybody can tell you that. Because I used to have a wonderful pair of lungs if I did say it myself. And he says, I don't hear the tuba, Chink. I look at him, I says, are you kidding, Mr. Biles Stoffer? He says, no, Chink. He says, no, Chink. He says, there's nothing comin' out of it. Man, I start to get worried. I look at him like that. Took the mouthpiece off. I had to get laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid laid I look at him and I say, are you kidding Mr. Beistoffer? He says, no, Chank. He says, there's nothing coming out of it. Man, I start to get worried. I start rubbing my lip like that. I look in the mouthpiece like that. I took the mouthpiece off. I took the slightest. Good grief. I said, don't tell me I'm breaking down. You see? Because I could see he was serious about it, you know? So I took the God-doin' thing off my neck and I put it down. See? Like that. And then I don't know what's making it. And I look down at the two of them. There's a big four of them. Two of them! Come on! Oh! Oh! Oh! Oh, man, Beist. I can't stand this no more. He says, that's no way to treat this man. This man, this man is blowing his lungs out there. Nothing coming out. Look at what. Who done this? He tried to fly. You could never fly. I don't die. Because I had it on the corner of the coach, you know? With the belt. You know, that corner right there. You know what he'd done? He just had to throw towels in there and shove them in with the head, you know? And I was blowing like that. Because to tell you the truth, I couldn't hear it myself. But I figured maybe it was my ears or something. The towels! And no wonder he couldn't hear it. And then, the entire time, the leg caught me. And I leave something that I never do. I leave the mouthpiece on the horn. And he takes a limb-boigert cheese and fills the mouthpiece with limb-boigert cheese. And naturally, sometimes, you know how we are in a hurry. All right, let's go. Grab that and I'll grab that and put it to my-
No, boy! What's the point?
No, boy! No, no, no, no. You know, man, I'm telling you, them fellas used to play rough. Yeah.
What about Abbey Brunies? Oh, well.
That was out of question. I couldn't tell you about him. I couldn't tell you about him.

That's not Abbey the drummer that died in New York. No, no. The trumpet player. No, the trumpet player. It's his uncle or his father? His uncle. No, Abbey Brunies the drummer played. That's what he used to play with chalky.
Yeah. He took mum's place. Yeah. I was supposed to meet him for dinner in New York the night he died. No kidding.
I was living up there then. Yeah. Well, I'm telling you, that was a rough element.
Well, Dick Allen was telling me that you once played some guitar duets with rap. Did he play the guitar duets?
Yeah, when we made that recording in Indianapolis, at the time, you know, with the big band, that you played some guitar duets with rap.

Yeah, when we made that recording in Indianapolis, at the time, you know, with the big band, that we, with New Orleans, Harlem Kings, we, rap and I played a duet with two guitars. He played the blues and I made the accompaniments, you know, behind him. But we made the recording, but I never heard anything of it. Did he play much? No, I never heard nothing of it. Did he play much? In fact, Carol Pierce, some of the musicians says they heard it, but I never did hear. Carol Pierce, I heard a piano, because we had three piano players when we went there. Carol Pierce made, he was a pianist, and he, from Strangton, he came from Strangton. And he made a number there, composed a number there by the name of Marguerite. Now, I made that number, but for, I mean, up until this, till this day, I never heard it. I've never heard it. Yeah, that's our record. Yeah, we have it. You got a record on it? Yeah.
Oh, no. Yeah. The guitar never came out though. Maybe it was a test record. You got Marguerite? Yeah. Yeah. Well, that goes to show it. A lot of people have that. Not a lot, but a few.
Yeah, I heard a couple of them tell me that they heard it.
If you want to hear it, you can come up and we'll dig all those things out up at Tulane, I'll show you. Some of the different stuff you got, or I can bring it down here, whatever you want.

Well, I swear, can you imagine a thing like that? And since I recorded that number, I heard all the rest of the numbers, but that one-size number I recorded. Yeah, I heard the record. Now, I heard the numbers of what we made with Jell-Ole Morton, because Jell-Ole Morton sat down and played his, you know, his compositions of Jell-Ole, and Saab and Blues, and some of that. Some of that are two or three numbers. I don't know who it was. But our real piano player at that time was Fritzl, Mike Fritzl, not Mike Fritzl. Mel Stitzel. Mel Stitzel. Mel Stitzel. I'm even getting mixed up with Mike Fritzl. Well, that's almost the same name. Yeah. Okay, he was the owner of the nightclub.
Friars Inn.
Friars Inn, yeah.
So how did rap play guitar? Did he ever play very much on it? I never really played.

No, just to specialize on blues, that's all. And just one string at the time. He didn't know no chords or nothing, but he just made a practice of that, you know. That's why I had to make the accompaniments on the guitar for what it was. Filled in the chords. But it was really nice. It was really nice. And I don't know for what reason, unless that we might have probably put in something there. Because you see, they only allow you so many measures of so on certain number. And if you go over that, because they can, after you, I believe it's after four measures, or eight measures of a number, like that, they consume you.
Oh yeah, if the melodies are saying that, yeah.
Now that's the only thing that I can see that, because the number was nice. It really, because we practiced on it, you know. But it never had come out.

Because they could have made a mistake there in the machine or something. Well, yeah, yeah, that's right. Maybe they made a test record and they just felt with a cell or something. That's right. Maybe they'll get something else, the band knows. Yeah, they'll get something happened or... They'll tell any reason. They can tell them. Did you ever know Don Murray? Played tenor saxophone. Yeah, Don Murray, sure. I just wondered if he made any records, would you always like them?
Don Murray, that I can remember, I made a recording with Don Murray, but where?
You recorded with several guys out there, different bands? Yeah.
Yeah, I recorded with, uh, uh, what is his name?
Oh, I can't take their names right off the wheel. What did the guy play? Saxophones.
Chicago band, right? Yeah, because mostly, mostly at that time, the range, the range were at the range, was the saxophones. Man, you heard most saxophones playing.
Yeah, but this is before, this is before Bud Friedman became very popular, I guess. Before Odd Castle. Oh, yeah. So even Wayne King played sax on those days, something like that.

Um... Valley Dufour. Oh, yeah. If I could think, if I want to get a chance to think of it like that, you know, it takes time. Yeah. It's so long, you know what I mean? Yeah. Now they talk about a good sax man. That's Zach Valley Dufour. He's a good clarinetist too, I've heard of. That's how I'm going to play clarinetist. Oh, yeah. You've got to end right of you. What was the place you wanted to ask about Dick's on the... Well, the Honeysuckle Inn? I always wondered why they called it the Honeysuckle Inn. That was old man Petrana's idea.
Honeysuckle.

Because the way they tell me, I don't know, but he used to have a house that all the... sides of his house, the fence was Honeysuckle Inn. And that's where you give it to Honeysuckle. I played there with Sharky, and I played with a joke about myself, Leo Eves, and Arthur Schellang.
Oh, Augie Schellang. The drummer, Augie Schellang. I remember Augie. That's another story.
I don't forgot it so long.

Did it have Honeysuckle on it, that place? Huh? It had Honeysuckle around it. No. No, they just give it the name. It's Honeysuckle. I don't know as much about all these things as Bill and Dick do. What part of town was the Honeysuckle Inn?
You remember at the end of the West End before you turned to go to the fountains? The Bucktown Inn? About Bucktown Inn. On the left-hand side.
Where the My Oh My Club is, out in that area.
No, My Oh My is all in Bucktown. This is before you hit Bucktown.
Before you hit Bucktown.
This was on the road going to West End. It was another bridge. It was about, I would say about two or three blocks before you hit the Black Bridge.
Uh-huh.

You know where the bridge is? Yeah, sure. Where you cross to go to the West End. Yeah. Just that. About two or three blocks. Uh-huh. And it was about two blocks back of the road. That was the Honeysuckle Inn. Oh, what? I went to so, I went to so many places. It's hard to find Tokyo Garden. I don't know. The Shim Sham. And the little club. In fact, I played almost in every club.
But the Cadillac Club. The Cadillac, no. That came along a little later, I guess. Francis Murray used to tell him about the wild scene in the Cadillac.

No, that's one club. I played one job at the Cadillac Club. That was for some kind of a private affair. But that was one night we played in the Cadillac Club. We're a different band all together. See you. But I mean all the rest of the clubs. I guess a hundred of them. Of course now, what we used to call the Timberline District. I never had one day with that at all. That was completely out of my line. I didn't like that.
Did you ever hear any hot fiddle players? That's what I was going to ask about.
Yeah, I heard. Hot fiddle players. Now you take like Oscar Marco. You take like Bonuti.
Did you play violin yourself?
You remember Bonuti? Oh yeah.
Did you play violin yourself? Yeah, I played violin.

And they used to have... Now wait, let me think. That's a 1900... 1913 or 1914. I used to live on Oiseline Street between an old man's house that used to have a grocery at that time where they got the drugstore on Royal and Oiseline. Am I right or wrong? Right. And I used to live in a backyard, an apartment upstairs. And there used to be a barber shop, no more than three or four doors from one that was run by a colored fellow. But he was so bright that he was what you would call a... What do you call an octo? He was like an octo. Yeah. He was colored, but he was bright. He was bright. You never would say it. And he was a violinist. And many times... He had a barber shop. He was a barber. And many times, him and I used to play guitar and he used to play violin, you know?
Was Dave Perkins very light too? Did you ever play with him? Yeah, Dave Perkins.
He was colored, I guess. Yeah, Dave Perkins is a fellow like me. You never would think that he had colored blood.
Who was that federal player? Who was the violin player? Batiste O'Quinn. Oh yeah, I heard of him from Jack Langan. Oh, you did?

Yeah. Mama Langan used to talk about him. Batiste O'Quinn. It goes to show you what I'm telling you. It's not no line because they can verify it, you know? But then it's all the men I played. And without counting the men that I've learned myself, you know? Learned them how to play bass. Learned them how to play guitar. Like you see that little instrumentation we had, a string ensemble we had of violin, guitar, and bass. When I was playing violin, and I had a little Puerto Rican day, he played guitar. And the bass player was named Frank Otero. Well, I learned them the instruments. And it was not long before that we used to play all these little joints on Decatur Street for those seamen's.
Did you ever have any of those old bands that, a dance band, a dance and jazz band that had an accordion in it? No.

Yeah, accordion, but the accordions that they had at that time, but it's not the accordions. Well, like a concertina I guess is that. No, that's it. It wasn't a concertina. It was a red accordion like they got there. Yeah. But they only had the natural notes. They had no sharps.
No full keyboard.
No full keyboard. In other words, it ran, I believe it was 16 notes, that's all. In accordion, and they only had two bass.
Is that right?
They had the tonic and the seventh, that's all.
So it was a lot smaller instrument then than what you were saying?
Yeah, well it was no bigger than that, and about that wide, and it stretched out that long. Uh-huh.
Is that like the Cajun Jews? Is that what they call a German accordion?

Yeah, yeah, that's it. The German accordion. I heard of them, but I haven't seen them. That's what they used to have at that time. Yeah. Well, I played with that, with accordion, guitar and bass. I played with accordion.
Did many of the dance bands have violins in them, most of them?

No, no dance bands. No violins at all. They didn't do it? All the dance bands that they had was just reed, brass, and string. I mean, it falls to bass, what do you call it? Yeah. But I mean, they didn't have the... But there was no such thing as violins or nothing. The first band that I played were a dance band that had a violin. That's when I tell you that I played at the Black Orchard, whose name the Black Orchard was Pete Hoyman's place. That's when we had Oscar Marco and his brother, Mickey Marco. You see? One played violin, the other one played...
But back in Jack Lane's days, he didn't use a violin... Well, yeah.

At one time, this fellow, the little guitar player, what they call him, little Joe Hernandez, he used to play a little violin himself, but mostly he played guitar. But it's very seldom that he used it. What about Watsky? He just used it now and then, you know what I mean?

What about Watsky? Did you ever know him? A violin player named Watsky? King, Watsky, got everybody to know him. He may have been uptown or something. No, I don't know. I think maybe Bud Lloyd Cannon told me about him or something. I'm not sure what I've been talking about. You know where I'm telling him.

Well, Dick, I might have... You see, this is the idea. I might have known him, but I just can't recollect the name, you see? I can't place the name. Sure, well, you never remember everybody's name. Because I've met so many and played with so many, I can't think of their names. You know what I mean?
Was Max Fink hot like Oscar Marco or was he more straight?
No, Max Fink was straight. And Max Fink had the most scientific G-string solo on his violin than anybody you ever heard in your life. I never heard a man play on a G-string on a violin like Max Fink.
Did he play in the theater here like the Art of Fame? Yeah, he played at the Liberty Theater. He played at the Little Club, didn't he?
Huh?
Didn't he play at the Little Club? He played at the Little Club too and then he played at the Liberty Theater. You mentioned a few minutes ago, Chene, about the...
Now, speaking about piano players, you're never going to get a piano player like Labosche. You heard about him?
He played with Perani?
Yeah.
Yeah, I heard about him.

There's a piano player you should avoid. Oh, I'm done. He had a hand on that piano that when he was just mad and he played on that piano, he'd break the strings on it. No kidding. He was so sure of that piano. He would never play the piano like that. You should never see him playing like that. That's the way he was... Yeah, really.
It's a better...
I'm telling you, that piano would be taking a beat. Yeah, lift his hand way up from the keys every time.
Labosche. Yeah. Really attack.
Wonderful piano.

Wonderful piano sport. You were mentioning, once again, just to improve my own knowledge in geography, you were mentioning not wanting to play in the district they call the Tenderloin. Now, is that Storyville or would that have been a different place at that time? Basin Street and all of them.
No, there's another piano stair that followed him, that Frank Cuehn. Uh-huh.
I've heard that name.
He just died.
Yeah. He just died. Yeah. No kid.
Yeah. Not long ago. A month or so ago. I think it was in the...

in the... in the... in the... in the... in the last... Yeah. I saw it in the paper. Yeah. What, they had it in the paper? Yeah. They had it in the paper. That you know. Up in Jefferson Parish. I think. Frank Cuehn.

That is another... Another wonderful musician. Another wonderful pianist. Trying to think what band he was with when I came to town. Yeah. We were... We were... He played with symphony, he played in all these theaters, in the Palace Theater and all that. When I came, he was with Detroit on some records. And Detroit, yeah.

Well when I was with Detroit, Freddie Newman was playing. Freddie Newman was the piano player with Detroit when I played with Detroit. Freddie Newman, yeah. Yeah, you played with Freddie Newman at the Bienville Roof, didn't you? Yeah.

Oh, I played with Freddie Newman plenty of times. I played with Freddie Newman. Freddie Newman was our piano player when we played at the ringside for Pete Whippen. And then when we played for, what is his name, I can't think of his name, he had a nightclub on Bienville Street.
Oh, hell, what is his name? Musician-only club?
No, he was an Italian.
Near the fern, around in that area? Is that the district or down here?

No, no, right here on Bienville Street between, I believe it was between Boybin and Dolphine, or both. No, the Dolphine, Bienville between Dolphine and Bergogne. It used to be a dying dancing hall. And this fella picked it up and made a nightclub on him. Trambina! Trambina. That's his name. That's Trambina. I'm coming around. He had a dress, then he opened, he closed that. Which is right now, what they call it, the forest cafe or whatever.
Oh yeah, I found it with Mustangs.
Yeah, well it was named the Silver Slipper.
Oh sure, that was the name of what I can't remember.
Well, I went to work then. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

segments.title: Opening: date, place and introductions
segments.summary: Interviewers state the date (October 19, 1966), location and interviewee Martin Abraham Sr., known as Chink Martin.

segments.title: First instrument: guitar lessons with Francisco Quinones
segments.summary: Martin's first instrument was guitar, taught by a Mexican bandsman who nicknamed him Chinito and wanted him to learn piano, which scared him off.

segments.title: Mexican and Spanish neighborhood in the French Quarter
segments.summary: Describes the Quarter streets populated by Mexicans, Puerto Ricans and Spaniards, later replaced by Italians, and his Spanish.

segments.title: Serenading with Mexican singers on guitar
segments.summary: He accompanied groups serenading sweethearts, played songs like La Guadalupana, and recalls a parody lyric.

segments.title: Where he lived and was born
segments.summary: He lived in the Quarter until about 30; he was born in Bayou St. John when luggers and schooners came in.

segments.title: His real birth date and the christening mistake
segments.summary: Born June 10, 1889 by his papers, but christened at three, so he thinks he is older; this caused trouble with the union card.

segments.chapter: Chicago union and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Joining the union and going to Chicago with the Rhythm Kings
segments.summary: He has been in the union since 1923; Rappolo invited him to join the New Orleans Rhythm Kings in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Chicago union and the Rhythm Kings
segments.title: Failing and then passing the Chicago union exam
segments.summary: Told the union was fixed, he failed his sight-reading exam, got a second chance from secretary Bankard, memorized the intro and passed.

segments.title: Did only Black musicians play early jazz? Tempo and race
segments.summary: Asked about white musicians in early jazz, he rejects the idea that Black players kept better tempo and says imitation is no good.

segments.title: Imitation tangent: Japanese Lewis imitators and Dr. Tichenor's
segments.summary: Ferguson tells a story about imitating George Lewis; Martin returns to tempo, which cannot be taught.

segments.title: Quinones's metronome training for tempo
segments.summary: The guitar professor trained students to hold tempo by covering the metronome and playing on.

segments.title: First white jazz band he heard: the High Rollers
segments.summary: He recalls hearing the High Rollers, a white ragtime band, around 1908; the word jazz was then a bad word.

segments.title: High Rollers members, Gallaty, Jack Laine and Frankie Christian
segments.summary: He lists the players in the High Rollers, the leader Bill Gallaty, and the bands that followed: Jack Laine and Frankie Christian.

segments.title: Tempo cannot be taught; it must come from the heart
segments.summary: Answering the claim that no whites played jazz before 1920, he says tempo is felt by dancers and cannot be learned.

segments.title: Modern drumming, fast tempos and Dixieland
segments.summary: He criticizes drum solos and fast tempos, contrasts old mediocre tempos with Dixieland and cites Armstrong's applause and the Famous Door.

segments.title: Real New Orleans jazz versus fast Dixieland; symphony benefit
segments.summary: They distinguish fast Dixieland from New Orleans jazz, and Martin recalls a show where the other band's members kept time to his.

segments.title: Quinones's advice: play from the heart
segments.summary: Quinones told him it is not what you do but how you do it.

segments.chapter: Playing bass in the early bands
segments.title: Why he dropped guitar and instrumentation of early bands
segments.summary: Guitar could not be heard with brass, banjos came in, and bands had trumpet, clarinet, trombone, bass and drums with no piano.

segments.chapter: Playing bass in the early bands
segments.title: Playing full chords on the bass
segments.summary: Dissatisfied with two beats to the bar, he played full chords on the bass to fill out the band; also notes on tailgate trombone.

segments.chapter: Playing bass in the early bands
segments.title: Roles in the ensemble: clarinet, ensemble and the Night Owls
segments.summary: He explains each instrument's role, with Ferguson's Pee Wee Spitelera story and the band's ensemble approach.

segments.title: Playing at the Ringside with Sharkey's band
segments.summary: He describes the Sharkey band at the Ringside for Pete Herman, its members, and his role running it.

segments.title: Early bands' musicianship and rough jobs
segments.summary: Early musicians were not accomplished, and he hints at rough stories not for tape.

segments.title: Shriner tour prank with Beiersdorffer's band
segments.summary: A Shriners tour with Johnny Bayersdorffer's band in which pranksters stuffed his tuba with towels and cheese.

segments.title: Abbie Brunies and rough characters
segments.summary: Brief exchange about the Brunies family and Abbie Brunies's death in New York.

segments.title: Guitar duet with Rappolo on the NORK Gennett session
segments.summary: He recalls the Indianapolis recording where he and Rappolo played guitar duets, Carol Pierce's Marguerite, and that the duet was never released.

segments.title: Other recordings and saxophone players
segments.summary: They ask about Don Murray and other recordings with Chicago bands, when saxophones were popular.

segments.title: Honeysuckle Inn, other clubs and Timberline district
segments.summary: He explains the Honeysuckle Inn's location near West End, plays with Sharkey there, and lists clubs he played, avoiding the Tenderloin.

segments.title: Hot fiddlers and his own string trios
segments.summary: Discusses violinists Oscar Marco, Dave Perkins, Batiste O'Quinn, and his own violin-guitar-bass groups on Decatur Street.

segments.title: Early accordions in dance bands
segments.summary: He describes small German accordions with natural notes and two basses, and playing with accordion, guitar and bass.

segments.title: Violins in dance bands; Max Fink
segments.summary: Dance bands rarely used violins; first with a violin was Pete Herman's Black Orchard with the Marco brothers; Max Fink was a straight violinist.

segments.title: Pianist Labosche
segments.summary: He praises a powerful pianist named Labosche who could break piano strings.

segments.title: Pianist Frank Cuehn
segments.summary: Talk of the late pianist Frank Cuehn who played in theaters and with symphony.

segments.title: Freddie Newman and the Silver Slipper club
segments.summary: Freddie Newman was his piano player at the Ringside, and he recalls the Italian-owned nightclub on Bienville Street.
